blocks.text: An aircraft's cabin-floor tie rod and a bridge's hanger cable both carry tension, yet the best material for one is not the best for the other, because one is limited by stiffness and the other by strength. A performance index turns that choice into a calculation.

blocks.markdown: Selecting a material by looking for the largest modulus, or the largest strength, rarely gives the best design, because the geometry can be adjusted. A systematic approach asks four questions. What does the component do (**function**)? What conditions must it meet (**constraints**)? What are we trying to minimise or maximise (**objective**)? What can we change (**free variables**)? The answers combine into a **performance index**, a group of material properties that ranks materials for that job.

blocks.caption: Four elements of a selection problem.

blocks.title: Performance index
blocks.text: A combination of material properties, $M$, that, when maximised, gives the best performance for a stated function, constraints and objective. It is obtained by eliminating the free variable between the constraint and the objective, and contains only material properties.

blocks.caption: Mass $m$ (kg), area $A$ (m$^2$), length $L$ (m), density $\rho$ (kg/m$^3$), Young's modulus $E$ (Pa), required stiffness $S^*$ (N/m).

blocks.title: Deriving the index for a light, stiff tie
blocks.prompt: Derive the performance index for a tie of fixed length $L$ and minimum stiffness $S^*$, with minimum mass.

steps.text: Write the objective in terms of the free variable $A$.
Use the constraint at its limit to find $A$.
The geometry and requirement ($S^*$, $L$) are fixed, so mass is smallest when $E/\rho$ is largest.

blocks.answer: The performance index is $M=E/\rho$ (specific stiffness): maximise it to minimise the mass.

blocks.title: Ranking materials for the tie
blocks.prompt: The tie has $L=2$ m and $S^*=5$ MN/m. Find the minimum mass for steel ($E=210$ GPa, $\rho=7850$ kg/m$^3$), aluminium alloy (70 GPa, 2700 kg/m$^3$), titanium (110 GPa, 4500 kg/m$^3$) and a carbon-fibre composite along its fibres (140 GPa, 1550 kg/m$^3$).
blocks.answer: The composite gives a tie about one-third of the mass of the metal ties; steel and aluminium are nearly equal, and titanium is the heaviest, which follows the $E/\rho$ ranking.

blocks.markdown: **Other loadings, other indices.** The index depends on the loading and the constraint. For a tie that must be *strong* rather than stiff, the constraint is no yielding, $F/A\le\sigma_y$. Then $A=F/\sigma_y$ and $m=FL\,\rho/\sigma_y$, so the index is $\sigma_y/\rho$. Bending changes the exponent because the section shape also matters: a light stiff beam of fixed section shape is ranked by $E^{1/2}/\rho$, and a light stiff panel by $E^{1/3}/\rho$.

blocks.caption: Common performance indices for minimum mass.

items: Identify the function, constraints, objective and free variables before looking at any data.
Eliminate the free variable using the constraint; what remains is a group of material properties.
Maximise (or minimise) the index; rank candidates by it, not by any single property.
Material choice may differ for different constraints on the same component.

blocks.title: Check by units
blocks.text: The index for the stiff tie is specific stiffness $E/\rho$ (GPa per Mg/m$^3$ or MN m/kg). If your derived index does not reduce to a ratio of material properties with no geometry left, a free variable was not eliminated.

points: A selection problem has a function, constraints, an objective and free variables; eliminating the free variable gives a performance index.
For a light, stiff tie, $m=S^*L^2\,\rho/E$, so maximise $E/\rho$; for a light strong tie maximise $\sigma_y/\rho$.
Rank candidates by the index and, if needed, compute the mass: the best material depends on the constraint.

questions.stem: In the design of a light, stiff tie rod of specified length $L$ that must have a minimum axial stiffness, which quantity is the free variable that is eliminated to obtain the performance index?

options.text: The cross-sectional area $A$ (together with the choice of material)

questions.correctOptionText: The cross-sectional area $A$ (together with the choice of material)

distractorRationale.a: Correct: $A$ is adjustable and is eliminated using the stiffness constraint.
distractorRationale.b: The length is specified, so it is a constraint, not a free variable.
distractorRationale.c: The mass is the quantity to be minimised, the objective, not a free variable.
distractorRationale.d: The required stiffness is a constraint fixed by the design brief.

questions.explanation: Free variables are the quantities the designer can change. Here the length and stiffness are fixed by the brief, the mass is the objective, and the section area is free, so it is eliminated between the constraint and the objective equations.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the objective in the tie-rod problem, as opposed to a constraint?

options.text: Minimise the mass of the tie
The tie must have a stiffness of at least $S^*$
The tie must carry an axial load

questions.correctOptionText: Minimise the mass of the tie

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the objective is the quantity to be minimised or maximised.
distractorRationale.b: This is a constraint on performance.
distractorRationale.c: A fixed length is a constraint.
distractorRationale.d: This describes the function, not the objective.

questions.explanation: Function says what the component does (carry tension); constraints are conditions that must be met (length, stiffness); the objective is what to minimise or maximise (mass, cost). Free variables, such as area, are what you can adjust to meet the constraints.

questions.stem: The mass of a tie of length $L$ and area $A$ is $m=AL\rho$, and its axial stiffness is $S=AE/L$. For a light tie of given stiffness, which index should be maximised?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: eliminating $A$ gives $m=S^*L^2\,\rho/E$, so minimum mass needs maximum $E/\rho$.
distractorRationale.b: This reverses the role of density; heavier material does not help.
distractorRationale.c: This is the quantity to minimise, not maximise.
distractorRationale.d: This is the index for a strong (not stiff) tie.

questions.explanation: The stiffness constraint $S=AE/L=S^*$ gives $A=S^*L/E$. Substituting in $m=AL\rho$ gives $m=S^*L^2\,(\rho/E)$, so the lowest mass comes from the largest $E/\rho$.

questions.stem: A tie must carry a given tensile force $F$ without yielding, at minimum mass. Which index should be maximised?

distractorRationale.b: This is the index when stiffness, not strength, is the constraint.
distractorRationale.c: This index relates to elastic strain at yield, not to mass.
distractorRationale.d: This is the reciprocal, which would be minimised.

questions.explanation: No yielding means $F/A\le\sigma_y$, so the smallest allowed area is $A=F/\sigma_y$. Then $m=AL\rho=FL\,(\rho/\sigma_y)$, which is minimised by maximising $\sigma_y/\rho$.

questions.stem: A tie of length 1.5 m must have an axial stiffness of at least 2.0 MN/m. A magnesium alloy ($E=45$ GPa, $\rho=1740$ kg/m$^3$, typical values) is proposed. Using $A=S^*L/E$ and $m=AL\rho$, calculate the minimum mass of the tie in kg.
questions.explanation: The required area is $A=S^*L/E=(2.0\times10^{6})(1.5)/(45\times10^{9})=6.667\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$ (66.7 mm$^2$). The mass is $m=AL\rho=6.667\times10^{-5}\times1.5\times1740=0.174$ kg.

questions.stem: For a light, stiff tie, a carbon-fibre composite along its fibres has $E/\rho=90.3$ GPa per Mg/m$^3$ ($E=140$ GPa, $\rho=1.55$ Mg/m$^3$), and a titanium alloy has $E=110$ GPa and $\rho=4.5$ Mg/m$^3$. For ties of the same length and stiffness, calculate the ratio of the titanium tie's mass to that of the composite tie (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: For fixed $S^*$ and $L$ the mass is proportional to $\rho/E$, so the mass ratio is the inverse ratio of the indices: $m_{Ti}/m_{C}=(E/\rho)_C/(E/\rho)_{Ti}=90.3/24.4=3.70$. The titanium tie is nearly four times heavier.

questions.stem: A tension tie of length 0.80 m must carry 20 kN without yielding. A steel with yield strength 350 MPa and density 7850 kg/m$^3$ is used, with no safety factor. Calculate the minimum mass of the tie in kg.
questions.explanation: The minimum area is $A=F/\sigma_y=20\,000/(350\times10^{6})=5.714\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$. The mass is $m=AL\rho=5.714\times10^{-5}\times0.80\times7850=0.359$ kg. A safety factor would multiply the area and mass accordingly.

questions.stem: Using the index $E/\rho$ for a light, stiff tie, rank these three candidates from best to worst. Values: glass-fibre composite ($E=40$ GPa, $\rho=1.9$ Mg/m$^3$); magnesium alloy ($E=45$ GPa, $\rho=1.74$ Mg/m$^3$); titanium alloy ($E=110$ GPa, $\rho=4.5$ Mg/m$^3$).

options.text: Magnesium alloy, titanium alloy, glass-fibre composite
Titanium alloy, magnesium alloy, glass-fibre composite
Glass-fibre composite, magnesium alloy, titanium alloy
Magnesium alloy, glass-fibre composite, titanium alloy

questions.correctOptionText: Magnesium alloy, titanium alloy, glass-fibre composite

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the indices are 25.9, 24.4 and 21.1 GPa per Mg/m$^3$.
distractorRationale.b: Titanium has the highest modulus but also a high density; its index (24.4) is below the magnesium alloy's (25.9).
distractorRationale.c: Its index is only 21.1, the lowest of the three.
distractorRationale.d: The glass-fibre composite (21.1) is below titanium (24.4), so this order is wrong.

questions.explanation: The indices are Mg alloy $45/1.74=25.9$, Ti alloy $110/4.5=24.4$ and glass composite $40/1.9=21.1$. Ranking by $E/\rho$ puts magnesium first, which shows that the highest modulus alone does not give the lightest tie.

questions.stem: A designer is asked to select a material for a light, stiff tie rod in a lifting frame. State the function, constraints, objective and free variables of the problem, and explain how the performance index is obtained from them.
markingGuide: Function: carry tension (axial load) as a tie (1 mark)
Constraints: specified length $L$; axial stiffness at least $S^*$ (and perhaps strength not exceeded) (2 marks)
Free variables: cross-sectional area $A$ and the choice of material (1 mark)
Index $M=E/\rho$ is to be maximised; it contains only material properties (1 mark)
questions.explanation: The index is found by writing the objective in terms of the free variable, using the constraint to eliminate the free variable, and grouping the material properties. For a stiffness-limited tie this gives $E/\rho$.

questions.stem: Three metals are candidates for a tension tie: a titanium alloy ($E=110$ GPa, $\sigma_y=900$ MPa, $\rho=4.43$ Mg/m$^3$), an aluminium alloy ($E=71$ GPa, $\sigma_y=500$ MPa, $\rho=2.8$ Mg/m$^3$) and a steel ($E=210$ GPa, $\sigma_y=1000$ MPa, $\rho=7.85$ Mg/m$^3$), all assumed typical values. Derive the index for a minimum-mass tie limited by strength, calculate both $\sigma_y/\rho$ and $E/\rho$, and show that the best material depends on the constraint.
markingGuide: Strength constraint $A=F/\sigma_y$ gives $m=FL\,\rho/\sigma_y$, so maximise $\sigma_y/\rho$ (2 marks)
Strength-limited best: titanium; stiffness-limited best: steel (1 mark)
Conclusion: the ranking depends on whether stiffness or strength is the constraint; this is why the constraint must be identified first (1 mark)
questions.explanation: The two constraints give different indices and different rankings: titanium has the best $\sigma_y/\rho$, but steel the best $E/\rho$ of the three. The same candidate list therefore gives different answers for different design problems.
